data.interpretation: The KPI has two parts. The main goal is to maximize the number of orders delivered town-wide within the promised SLA times (120 s order-to-pickup, 120 s pickup-to-delivery), which maps directly to on_time_deliveries. The second part, 'no company's customers should be kept waiting badly', is a fairness floor across companies A, B and C. It can be read in two ways: as a hard floor on the worst company's on-time rate (min_company_on_time_rate), or as a limit on the spread between companies (on_time_rate_gap). It also implicitly covers orders that are very late or never delivered (late_deliveries, unfinished). The KPI fixes the promised times, so loosening DELIVERY_SLA is not a legitimate way to raise the count. Any SLA change would be a contract decision for humans.

options.label: Maximize town-wide on-time deliveries with a floor on the worst company

goals.text: Primary: number of orders delivered within the promised 120 s + 120 s windows, town-wide.
Watch: on-time rate of the worst-served company must not fall.
Watch: orders left undelivered at period end, so late orders are not simply abandoned.
Watch: late deliveries should not grow as on-time count rises.

guards.text: Every company's customers get at least 80% on-time service (provisional reading of 'not kept waiting badly'; to be calibrated against the baseline).
No more than 3 orders left undelivered at period end (provisional; to be calibrated against the baseline).

options.note: Most direct reading. Total throughput is the target, and fairness is a hard floor rather than something to optimize. The threshold values are placeholders until baseline measurements are available.

options.label: Maximize the worst company's on-time rate (maximin fairness first)

goals.text: Primary: raise the on-time rate of the worst-served company.
Watch: town-wide on-time deliveries must not drop.
Watch: orders left undelivered at period end.

guards.text: No more than 3 orders left undelivered at period end (provisional).

options.note: Fits if the operator considers the fairness sentence the real priority. This option may accept smaller gains in total throughput.

options.label: Maximize town-wide on-time deliveries with a cap on the inter-company gap

goals.text: Watch: spread between best and worst company on-time rates.
Watch: worst company's on-time rate must not fall.

guards.text: Best and worst company on-time rates differ by at most 15 percentage points (provisional).

options.note: Reads 'no company kept waiting badly' as relative equality. The gap can be narrowed by making the best company worse, so the min rate is also watched.

concerns: 'Kept waiting badly' is not quantified. It could mean an absolute floor per company, a limit on the spread between companies, or no orders left undelivered. The numeric thresholds in the guards are provisional guesses and should be set from baseline measurements.

on_time_deliveries is a proxy that ignores orders already past their deadline. Optimizing it alone could deprioritize late orders and leave them unfinished, which is exactly the badly-kept-waiting outcome the KPI forbids. unfinished and late_deliveries are therefore watched or guarded.
on_time_rate_gap can be reduced by degrading the best company rather than helping the worst, which would hurt the town-wide goal. A floor via min_company_on_time_rate is safer.
Maximizing the town-wide total and protecting the worst company can conflict. For example, rules that favor the busiest company's routes may raise the total while starving another company.

The promised times (120 s / 120 s) are part of the KPI and of DELIVERY_SLA. Raising the on-time count by loosening the SLA would game the metric, and any SLA change must be decided by humans as a contract amendment.
